item.title: From KMS Auto to Scareware: Tracking a Multi-Stage Intrusion Linked to APT36?
item.description:
A cracked KMS activation tool seeds a multi-day intrusion chain ending in APT36-branded scareware, with XMRig, ScreenConnect, and MeshAgent deployed as stepping stones across 12-24 hour intervals.
Key findings:
- KMS Auto executed from an untrusted source served as the initial access vector (T1204.002). What looked like a routine software activation event was the entry point for a staged compromise. The critical forensic tell is not the tool itself but where it ran from and what child processes followed. Execution from unusual directories with subsequent miner or RAT activity should immediately escalate triage priority.
- XMRig deployed post-compromise for cryptocurrency mining (T1496), followed hours later by ScreenConnect dropped to C:\ProgramData\HvHosts\ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe and C:\ProgramData\OneDriveServer\OneDriveServer\OneDriveServer\ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe. MeshAgent was then added as a redundant backdoor. The consistent 12-24 hour staging interval between each capability drop is a behavioral signature worth hunting across endpoint telemetry.
- The final payload, SecurityHealthServices.exe, masquerades as a Windows Defender process (T1036.005) and lands in %ProgramData%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup for persistence (T1547.001). It carries APT36 and Transparent Tribe Pakistan 🇵🇰 branding in its metadata and icon, changes the desktop wallpaper to a Pakistani 🇵🇰 flag, and throws a locked overlay screen. Despite the ransomware theater, no file encryption occurs. It appends a second .exe extension to filenames and drops self-copies with super-hidden attributes into AppData (T1564.001). The ransom note contains no wallet address, no payment deadline, and no contact channel, which is the clearest indicator this is scareware, not ransomware.
- Attribution to APT36 (Transparent Tribe, Mythic Leopard, COPPER FIELDSTONE) is not confirmed by K7 Labs. The metadata and branding could be planted misdirection. The overall pattern, a home user hit by a cracked tool leading to a mining and RMM chain capped with a psychological payload, does not match APT36's known surgical espionage tradecraft against military and diplomatic targets. Treat the APT36 label as an artifact of the payload, not a confirmed attribution.
- Five hashes are listed in the IOC table: three Trojan detections tied to the scareware payload, one CryptoMiner detection for the XMRig component, and one RemoteTool detection for ScreenConnect. Full IOC list is in the report.
Hunt for the staging pattern: KMSAuto execution outside system directories, followed within 24 hours by XMRig process creation, then ScreenConnect or MeshAgent installation, then a new Startup folder entry named SecurityHealthServices.exe. Cross-reference Run and RunOnce registry keys and the C:\Users\Public\Recovery path for dropped batch scripts, VBS files, and XML configs. The double-.exe extension rename on non-encrypted files is a low-cost sweep for active scareware infections. Full IOC list is in the K7 Labs report.

item.title: CLOSEDQUORUM: Malware Puts AI in the C2 Loop
item.description:
CLOSEDQUORUM is the first publicly documented Windows implant to replace human C2 tasking with a commercial LLM voting panel, delegating tactical attack decisions to DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral, and Google Gemini in sequence.
Key findings:
- The implant is a 16.4 MB, 64-bit Go executable discovered by Cisco Talos through its CAIRN project. At initialization it collects hostname, OS architecture, CPU count, Windows version, privilege status, and current target process, then sends that host context to up to four LLM providers. Each model returns a structured JSON response selecting the next action. Plurality vote wins. Ties resolve deterministically by provider order: DeepSeek, then Qwen, then Mistral, then Gemini. If all providers fail, the implant sleeps and retries rather than defaulting to a capability.
- The LLM decision layer selects from a constrained action set. "steal" triggers simultaneous LSASS credential dumping, saved credential theft from Chrome, Edge, and Firefox, and cryptocurrency wallet theft from MetaMask, Exodus, and Ethereum stores. Stolen data is encrypted with AES-256-GCM and exfiltrated via Discord webhook. "inject" invokes shellcode and routes to either process hollowing or Early Bird APC injection. "persist" invokes persistence routines, and Talos identifies WMI persistence creation as a correlatable behavior. A "move" decision exists in the schema but has no implemented handler in the analyzed build.
- The publicly distributed binary is an inert template with placeholder LLM API keys and a dummy Discord webhook. Talos assesses the operating model as a configurable service: operators compile a custom build with their own credentials before deployment, and stolen credentials flow back through their Discord channel, effectively a credentials-as-a-service offering with autonomous LLM orchestration as the differentiator. Developer artifacts link to criminal-forum carding activity dating to 2025. No confirmed in-the-wild deployment has been observed.
- The architectural significance is the effort displacement model. The LLMs are not writing exploits or inventing attack paths. They are choosing among predefined capabilities the developer already coded, using host context as input. This removes the human operator from a bounded decision loop and allows the implant to continue executing while the attacker is offline. The same pattern is extensible to other intrusion phases, and it routes all C2 traffic through legitimate commercial AI infrastructure rather than attacker-controlled domains or IPs, putting pressure on detections that depend on known-bad destinations.
Six SHA-256 hashes are listed in the report: 250d4fa37488af9b025333fa17705573d721467b203765bc360890b4f5a90cd7, c4dc171f2513fcaf9d5ecc815a94aee4063b213ab380f80bd3ac422dee5205a7, c13cea04f598e2b0c248d603a6e31bd13aabb64d8149c1b6a77b64e0b983a86f, f5f1f8c3e7b883793800ab6ccf21b3e60bd0730f300b4595fe74a33adc17a63c, 5191cf625dfc209a347f137b50aea199e82040fd5ee9086fb3e2de73c133f3cb, and eddbd0ecf7195d38fefae5b9d393abfa79e6f3f94bde19308ecef130a05a42e5.
Hunt for Go-compiled 64-bit executables making outbound HTTPS to LLM provider API endpoints alongside concurrent Discord webhook POST traffic. Correlate with LSASS access events, WMI subscription creation, and process hollowing indicators such as a spawned suspended process followed by WriteProcessMemory and ResumeThread calls. Wallet and browser credential paths in AppData are the on-disk artifacts to triage. The implant's LLM dependency also means API key strings embedded in a binary are a detection surface worth adding to your triage playbook.

item.title: Detections Digest #20260928
item.description:
Weekly detection engineering roundup: 80 new rules and 43 updates across 11 repositories cover RMM abuse, LSASS dumping, email evasion, BYOVD, and Kubernetes container threats from Sep 21-28, 2026.
Key findings this week:
- RMM abuse detection expanded significantly via magicsword-io/LOLRMM and RussianPanda95/Yara-Rules, with 41 new rules covering process creation, file artifacts, registry persistence under Run keys and service installation paths, and outbound network connections for tools including Zecurit, Allocentra, OpenDesk, RMMCRAT, BlackCrypt, LightRmmAgent, and RemoteAgentAgent. A new YARA rule for RMMCRAT specifically targets PE headers combined with embedded RMMC and RMM Agent configuration strings. The generic DNS rule covering known RMM infrastructure was also refreshed with updated domain and IP indicators. Hunt for agent binaries in AppData, ProgramData, and Program Files alongside Run key writes and outbound DNS to unfamiliar cloud hosting endpoints.
- LSASS and token access detections in splunk/security_content and SigmaHQ/sigma moved from static GrantedAccess string matching to bitwise evaluations against Sysmon Event ID 10 telemetry. This matters because minor mask variations broke prior rules. Updated rules now cover read permissions on lsass.exe, Winlogon duplicate handle access, WMI token impersonation via wmiprvse.exe, and injection into notepad.exe. The Dumpert LSASS dumper detection shifted to IMPHASH-based matching rather than MD5 or command-line paths, which are trivially modified. Cross-reference Sysmon Event ID 10 bitwise access masks with process lineage and file_path fields for Task Manager dump artifacts.
- Email evasion coverage in sublime-security/sublime-rules received 12 new and 12 updated rules. New detections parse .ics calendar invites with oversized guest lists carrying voicemail, purchase order, missed call, and BEC lures, and decode hex-obfuscated recipient strings embedded in URL fragments and QR codes across PDF, ICS, and image attachments. Rules also flag Google Cloud Storage links to short HTML paths, newly registered domains on suspicious TLDs serving single-character HTML files, client-side JavaScript beaconing visitor tokens via dynamic Image objects, and Teams help desk impersonation correlated with mail bombing within a one-hour window. Updated rules unwrap Mimecast-protected links and refresh Spamhaus ASN-DROP coverage, removing prefixes tied to AS63023 and AS62563.
- BYOVD and in-memory defense evasion coverage updated across magicsword-io/LOLDrivers, rabbitstack/fibratus, and kevoreilly/CAPEv2. LOLDrivers rules added MD5, SHA1, SHA256, and IMPHASH values alongside driver filenames in ImageLoaded telemetry to catch hypervisor-protected code integrity bypasses. Four Fibratus rules for process hollowing, ghostly hollowing, activation context manipulation, and NTDLL remapping via file mapping were updated for engine version 3.2.0, refining section type filters including IMAGE and IMAGE_NO_EXECUTE. A new YARA rule in CAPEv2 detects Defendnot, a tool that impairs Windows Defender, via PE magic bytes and characteristic debug strings.
- Kubernetes container threat detection expanded through benscha/KQLAdvancedHunting with 13 new KQL rules querying CloudProcessEvents and CloudAuditEvents in Microsoft Defender XDR. Coverage includes reverse shells using network redirection, XMRig and Kinsing cryptominer execution, first-seen container binary baselining, container escape via nsenter, chroot, unshare, and socket interaction, service account token and ca.crt file reads, Kubernetes secret enumeration across namespaces, cluster-admin role binding creation, and deployment from unapproved registries. GitOps controllers ArgoCD and Flux are excluded to reduce noise. A new jkerai1 rule monitors AzureActivity for modifications to Azure public and private DNS zones, a low-visibility path adversaries use for traffic redirection.
Practitioner takeaway: the shift from static hash and string matching to bitwise access mask evaluation in LSASS rules is the most operationally significant change this week, since it closes a known evasion gap. Prioritize pulling updated Sysmon Event ID 10 rules from splunk/security_content and SigmaHQ/sigma into your pipeline. For RMM hunting, stack process, file path, registry, and network rules together rather than running them in isolation: a single layer is easy to miss, four correlated layers is a detection story. Full rule sets, IOCs, and YARA content are available in the linked repositories.

item.title: NeedyMantis: Unpacking a post-compromise malware family used in targeted operations
item.description:
NeedyMantis is a modular, post-compromise C++ and shellcode framework linked to Chinese 🇨🇳 threat actors, hitting telecoms, universities, and government contractors since at least October 2025.
- Storm-3069 is the named operator Microsoft associates with NeedyMantis, tied to the DAEMON Tools supply chain compromise previously reported by Kaspersky. Microsoft has not attributed Storm-3069 to a Chinese 🇨🇳 nation-state but notes all observed activity aligns with Chinese 🇨🇳 interests and selective deployment patterns. Additional NeedyMantis activity beyond Storm-3069 suggests more than one operator may have access to the framework.
- The delivery chain starts with DLL sideloading: a malicious first-stage loader masquerades as a legitimate DLL (WinSparkle.dll, libcurl.dll, vim64.dll, dbghelp.dll, jli.dll, nvml.dll) dropped alongside real software such as Poedit, curl, Vim, or TightVNC. The archive holding the payloads uses a custom XOR-encoded, RtlDecompressBuffer-compressed file format with per-sample offsets and keys. One observed incident used Impacket to copy the malicious bundle from a network share and execute it on a target host. The first-stage loader SHA-256 is e842dd7642c8e04b5ec20b6393848a9c904e4832930950c16664fe7800ba382e, and the WinSparkle archive is 9cb68f986043a576e19d32184c583b7d8f571c7219d8dc0065dced1c13f077ef.
- A file named encryptbase64.ps1 (actually x64 shellcode despite the extension) serves as the second-stage loader, decoding an embedded payload using ROR-based API hashing with rotation value 11. The main component loads configuration from a file named dnsapi.dll (not the real Windows DLL) and the communications module from ws2_32.dll (also fake). C2 is corp.tripswithengine[.]com on port 443 via URI /library/zip/. The initial beacon is an HTTPS GET where system information (hostname, username, process list, ProgramFiles contents) is Base64 and RtlCompressBuffer-encoded into a Set-Cookie header. The session upgrades to WebSockets, then a binary protocol with RC4 encryption keyed from a 1024-byte random buffer exchanged at handshake. The hard-coded user-agent is firefox/21.0, a reliable hunt anchor.
- The main component creates a mutex formatted as username-processname (e.g., Contoso-Poedit.exe) and supports dynamic module loading and unloading via commands 1020 and 1030, making the full capability set unknown until modules are recovered from operator infrastructure. Config, communications, and shellcode loader are all stored inside the custom archive as files with spoofed Windows system DLL names.
Hunt priority: query for the spoofed DLL paths (WinSparkle.dll in Poedit dirs, libcurl.dll under ProgramData\USOShared, vim64.dll under ProgramData\VIM or TightVNC\VIM, dbghelp.dll under ProgramData\office or broadcom, jli.dll under ProgramData\Intel, nvml.dll under ProgramFiles\modifiable or ProgramData\ics), outbound connections or any log entries referencing corp.tripswithengine[.]com, and user-agent string firefox/21.0 in proxy and firewall logs. The mutex pattern username-processname is a host-based artifact worth sweeping for. Microsoft's report includes KQL hunting queries for Defender XDR and Sentinel, plus the full IOC table and Microsoft Defender Antivirus detections (TrojanDropper:Win64/NeedyMantis, Behavior:Win64/NeedyMantis).

item.title: Quarantined isn't contained: Agentic phishing response with Elastic and Sublime
item.description:
Siloed email and endpoint alerts let phishing campaigns hide in plain sight. An agentic integration between Elastic and Sublime Security closes that gap, correlating quarantine events with endpoint telemetry and enabling bidirectional response without tool-switching.
Key findings:
- The core visibility problem is timing and context. A Sublime Security quarantine at 9:00 a.m. and a suspicious PowerShell process at 9:05 a.m. on the same host each look benign in isolation. Neither tool sees the other's signal, so the campaign opener goes uninvestigated. The native Elastic integration pulls Sublime telemetry (what was flagged, why, who was targeted, and what Sublime did) into Elastic Security alongside endpoint, identity, and network data, letting detection rules run across the combined dataset rather than each half separately.
- Attack Discovery acts as the agentic first pass. Once alerts stack up, Attack Discovery correlates them into unified attack chains by hunting for related activity, reading individual alerts, checking entity context, and querying raw logs across the platform. The output is a prioritized, evidence-grounded account of what happened, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK, with the reasoning visible to the analyst, not a raw queue to triage.
- The bidirectional SOAR integration is the containment multiplier. If Elastic Defend identifies malware on a host, a workflow can take that file's SHA-256 hash and trigger a blast-radius quarantine back in Sublime Security, pulling the same indicator from every mailbox it reached. The response flows from endpoint finding to email-side containment without leaving Elastic. The reverse also applies: a Sublime quarantine event can seed an Elastic case and push a Slack notification with the supporting evidence already attached for analyst review.
- Human-in-the-loop controls are per-action, not system-wide. Elastic Workflows lets teams set the automation threshold at the individual action level. A blast-radius mailbox quarantine, which is high-impact and difficult to reverse, routes through analyst approval. Low-impact enrichment or tagging steps can run automatically. The recommended approach is to start with maximum human review, compare the agentic recommendations against analyst judgment over time, and expand automation incrementally as trust builds.
Practitioner takeaway: The rollout path matters. Stage one is getting Sublime telemetry flowing into Elastic so existing detection rules immediately gain email context with no workflow changes required. Stage two is enabling the bidirectional SOAR actions after you have decided which responses run automatically and which require approval. When a SHA-256 hash from an Elastic Defend alert becomes the seed for a cross-mailbox quarantine, the artifact to preserve is the chain of evidence linking the endpoint event to the original email telemetry record. That linkage is what justifies the blast-radius action and what an IR review will need. Full integration documentation and workflow guidance are in the report.

item.title: Storm-3168, Linked to JADEPUFFER, Abused Stolen Azure Identities
item.description:
Storm-3168, tracked by Sysdig as JADEPUFFER, used two stolen Azure service principals to destroy over 100 storage accounts in seven minutes and harvest keys, in what Sysdig called the first documented agentic ransomware operation.
Key findings:
- The initial access vector is the headline forensic lesson. Credentials (client ID, client secret, and tenant ID) for one of the compromised service principals were posted in plaintext in a public GitHub issue by an employee of the victim organization. The issue was later edited to remove the secret, but GitHub preserves the full edit history, leaving the credentials accessible. Microsoft explicitly could not confirm this was the route used, but the warning is unambiguous: removing a post does not invalidate the credential. Defenders should treat any secret visible in public edit history as fully compromised and requiring immediate revocation, not just redaction.
- The attack split work across two service principals from the same tenant to separate reconnaissance from destruction. The first identity spent 15 hours 30 minutes completing more than 300 read operations. Ninety minutes later, the second enumerated the same environment across two subscriptions in five seconds. Both used the same Storm-3168 infrastructure, the same network fingerprint, and the user agent python-requests/2.34.2, a consistent behavioral signature across the operation. Overlapping token streams and precise inter-operation timing point to fully scripted or automated execution.
- The destructive phase lasted approximately seven minutes inside a 35-minute window of more than 150 destructive and credential-related operations. The second identity attempted deletion of over 100 storage accounts, a Key Vault, a Function App, and an App Service plan. It also targeted Azure Site Recovery and Azure Backup protection locks, and prioritized storage accounts with names referencing Terraform and backups, signaling deliberate recovery interference. Azure resource locks and deletion protection stopped several deletions, demonstrating that independent controls survive even broad Contributor-level compromise.
- Thirty minutes after the last deletion, the identity returned for keys. More than 30 successful ListKeys requests followed, including against Azure Site Recovery-linked accounts. One storage account in the same resource group as the deleted Key Vault was deliberately spared during destruction, then hit with a successful key request afterward, suggesting staged data theft preparation rather than pure destruction.
- The three IP addresses linked to Storm-3168 probing and malicious requests are 45.131.66[.]106, 34.153.223[.]102, and 64.20.53[.]230. Separate scanning from the same infrastructure targeted Azure App Services across different customers, hitting WordPress admin paths, PHP-CGI, and the LangFlow code validation endpoint at /api/v1/validate/code. None of those probes reached the affected subscriptions.
Hunt your Azure Activity Logs for ListKeys operations on storage accounts following resource deletion events, especially within the same resource group and within 30 minutes of destructive activity. Flag any service principal using python-requests/2.34.2 making bulk read operations. Audit service principal permissions for overly broad Storage Account Contributor or Contributor roles and cross-reference against GitHub, public issue trackers, and repository histories for exposed client secrets. Full IOC details and Microsoft's defensive guidance are in the report.

item.title: ShinyHunters Breached the FBI by Bypassing the Fix by Lucie Cardiet
item.description:
ShinyHunters breached the FBI's jobs portal via an unpatched Oracle PeopleSoft flaw, bypassing a published firewall workaround to steal agent PII and pivot into AWS government cloud storage.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-35273 is the Oracle PeopleSoft vulnerability at the center of this. Oracle patched it June 10, 2026, following Mandiant's report of zero-day exploitation against universities. Organizations that only applied the recommended firewall rule as a temporary control were not protected: by September, ShinyHunters had identified a single-character substitution in the web request that caused the firewall rule to miss the attack entirely while PeopleSoft processed it normally. The patch closed the hole; the workaround did not.
- The attack chain here is meaningfully different from ShinyHunters' prior campaigns. Earlier operations, including the Anodot/Snowflake wave and related helpdesk social engineering runs, relied on stolen credentials, token theft from SaaS integration providers, or MFA reset abuse. The login succeeded and looked legitimate. The FBI breach required no password at all: exploitation of a publicly accessible web application established a foothold directly on the server, then pivoted into FBI-managed Amazon government cloud storage. If your detection logic is tuned for post-authentication anomalies, you are watching the wrong layer for this intrusion class.
- Mandiant tracks this activity as UNC6240. ShinyHunters is the name on the leak site. Those are not interchangeable designations, and conflating them obscures which operators ran which campaigns and through which infrastructure. The report notes that when Scattered Spider, Lapsus$, and ShinyHunters announced they were going dark last September, the techniques and infrastructure did not follow. Operator branding changes; access methods persist.
- Scope of the September wave is broader than the FBI headline. Mandiant observed compromised PeopleSoft systems across higher education, technology, healthcare, agriculture, transportation, and government organizations globally. The FBI case has press; the others are being worked through quietly. ShinyHunters claims 2 to 3 terabytes exfiltrated from the FBI portal and downstream storage. The FBI has confirmed only that it is investigating.
- The group's stated motivation breaks from their pattern. Rather than a financial ransom, they published a PSA on their dark web leak site demanding the FBI retract or remove a May 2026 advisory that attributed harassment, swatting, and sextortion tactics to them. The deadline was September 30. The advisory remains up as of publication. Using stolen government personnel data as leverage against law enforcement's own public documentation is a different threat model than a standard pay-or-leak demand, and it changes what escalation looks like in the response timeline.
Practitioner takeaway: If you run Oracle PeopleSoft, the only confirmed protection is the patch for CVE-2026-35273 released June 10. Firewall-only mitigations are bypass-able as of September and should not be treated as closed controls. On already-exposed systems, Mandiant's follow-up report published September 25 covers what to look for on potentially compromised hosts. For hunting, the pivot from a PeopleSoft web tier into cloud-hosted storage is your lateral movement signal: look for outbound connections and data staging activity originating from the PeopleSoft application server process, not from an identity event. Full remediation guidance is in the Mandiant report.
